Discussions of medical insurance costs in the US often focus on the cost of drugs or the activities of large insurance companies. To have an informed debate, it is important to understand the structure of medical care supply and demand. 

Consider one aspect of health-care provision: the number of active physicians. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, there are approximately one million registered physicians of whom 866,000 are engaged in direct patient care. 

In discussing the formation of new physicians, we combined two facts: the total number of medical students is 100,000 *and* medical school takes four years. This led to our estimate that there will be 25,000 graduates each year. 
Revisit this model taking into account that not all entering medical students graduate. Assume that attrition in the first year is 10%, then 5% in each of the two successive years. 

If there are 100,000 students all together, how many graduate each year?

:::
